 Why Nvidia stopped telling investors about Singapore sales after cutting off Alice Huang-linked Megaspeed

 TOI Tech Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 12, 2026, 11:07 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print Nvidia stopped reporting Singapore sales after cutting off Megaspeed Nvidia quietly stopped reporting its Singapore revenue in late 2025, months after it cut off Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based cloud company now at the heart of the espionage scandal around CEO Jensen Huang. The timing, flagged by The Wall Street Journal, raises fresh questions about how much investors could see of Nvidia’s sales tied to a market that was briefly one of its biggest. In the quarter ending July 2025, Singapore brought in $10.2 billion, or 22% of Nvidia’s total revenue, up 81% from a year earlier. Two years before that, its share was just 8%. A quarter later, the line had vanished from Nvidia’s filings. An Nvidia spokesperson told the WSJ that Megaspeed was put on an internal block list in June 2025, barring further sales and shipments. The company has not said whether the two moves are connected. Nvidia switched from billing address to headquarters for country-wise revenue 
 From the quarter ending October 2025, Nvidia began assigning revenue by where a customer is headquartered rather than where it is billed. It said the change “provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue.” The old breakdown listed the US, Singapore, Taiwan, China (including Hong Kong) and “other”. The new one kept every line except Singapore. Recast figures suggest most Singapore-billed revenue moved into the US column, while China and Taiwan were revised higher. The WSJ points to a hole in that logic. Nvidia had earlier said Singapore was used mainly for centralised invoicing, with products “almost always shipped elsewhere.” A headquarters address says no more about where chips land. Nvidia spokesperson Patrick Rutherford declined to say where Megaspeed’s sales were booked under either method, or whether dropping Singapore was linked to the block. Servers from US firms like Dell and Super Micro add another layer. Many buyers get Nvidia chips inside these systems, and it is unclear whether those deals count as US revenue wherever the machines end up. Megaspeed probe and Alice Huang affair now threaten Jensen Huang’s job 
 In August 2025, between the block and the reporting change, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter emailed Commerce Department agents investigating Megaspeed, saying a senior department official had cleared him to reach out, according to The New York Times. The case was soon handed to the Justice Department, which is running a criminal inquiry. In October 2025, President Trump was briefed that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was presumed to be a Chinese intelligence asset close to Jensen Huang, the NYT reported. Trade records cited by the NYT show Megaspeed’s Malaysian sister firm Speedmatrix bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, well past the June 2025 cutoff and often through intermediaries. Megaspeed denies illegally moving chips to China. Huang has since admitted the affair and apologised to employees. Nvidia’s board is investigating whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and the WSJ has reported that the board is preparing to oust him. Without a Singapore line, Nvidia’s filings cannot show whether cutting off Megaspeed dented sales or barely registered. Either answer would have invited the questions the company is now facing anyway.
